doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Hearing Monk, Elvin and Dizzy live
summary: Nussbaum and Wall recall Monk's sound and Wall hears Elvin; Nussbaum remembers seeing Dizzy at age eight.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: ability of his sound to project was like getting hit with a hammer wrapped in velvet. I mean he was so loud. It was deceptive. You’d never get that from a record. You’d never get it. And like when I first heard Thelonious Monk live I could not believe how much sound he got out of the piano without banging. It was like there was mac trucks behind each finger putting out the sound. Astounding.

Yeah I remember that too, the first time I heard Monk at the Vanguard. Because that’s a good example of drawing a sound out of the instrument. It’s not done with force and attack and this and that. He was pulling the sound out. Or hearing Elvin live the first time.

Yeah I mean you can’t believe it. You just can’t believe being in that room. I mean and whenever there’s an opportunity I think for young musicians to go out, go out and see the old guys first. Because they’re not going to be around forever. I mean you will never forget it.
Plus you’re not seeing any of the — when you listen to a record you’re not seeing any of the body language and the eye contact and the way the music is shaped from the start of the song to the end.
Sure. If you’re in the room, that’s when I said it’s reality. You’re in the room, this is it, this is the whole picture, the complete picture is delivered to you.

Right. I mean and when you feel that amazing feeling from records, the records we all know and love that have helped to shape our whole reality as far as the way we perceive music and play, if you get that vibe from a record, imagine what it must have been like live. I mean so I can’t, it’s really important for young musicians to not just look at the books and look at the videos, but whenever there’s a chance, go out and see the cats play. There’s nothing like it. I mean I remember seeing Dizzy when I was eight years old. It was amazing. And he was amazing because he was just such a silly person and a great life force coming from this guy. I don’t even remember the music, I just remember this guy being so much fun and clowning around with me. Because the effect, the positive effect that that had on me as a kid made me then think about the music and like wow, this was something that gave me a great feeling. And then later on I was listening and I realized this guy was also a phenomenal musician but I just remembered him, as the human being, and just his vibe. And years later I was fortunate and I got to hang with Dizzy a bunch and I got to know him a little bit, and then I finally did get to play with him. And I said man you know when I was eight years old I saw you play and it was at this gig at Leonard Bernstein’s house for the NAACP, a benefit, in like the 60s. And Wes Montgomery was there, Morgana King, Milt was there, Billy Taylor, and Dizzy was there. And there was no bandstand, they were just set up like on a platform.
